# Working Summary

The Comparative Observer Test begins with:

```text
TARGET STRUCTURE
       +
OBSERVER A
       ↓
OBSERVATION A
```

and:

```text
TARGET STRUCTURE
       +
OBSERVER B
       ↓
OBSERVATION B
```

Then:

```text
COMPARE
   ↓
FIND INVARIANTS
   ↓
LOCATE FIRST DIVERGENCE
   ↓
IDENTIFY OBSERVER CONDITIONS
   ↓
IDENTIFY NON-OBSERVER VARIABLES
   ↓
GENERATE ALTERNATIVES
   ↓
DEFINE A DISCRIMINATOR
   ↓
REPEAT
   ↓
REVISE
```

Its permanent guardrails are:

```text
DIFFERENCE
    ≠
OBSERVER EFFECT PROVEN
```

```text
AGREEMENT
    ≠
TRUTH
```

```text
DISAGREEMENT
    ≠
RELATIVITY
```

```text
TRIADIC OBSERVER
    ≠
FORCED SYNTHESIS
```

```text
MISSING VARIABLE
    ≠
HIDDEN OBSERVER PROVEN
```

```text
LOCAL OBSERVATION
    ≠
GLOBAL CLAIM
```

The guiding discipline is:

> **Hold the target as stable as practical.  
> Preserve each observer's first response independently.  
> Separate observation from interpretation.  
> Find what the observers share before focusing only on disagreement.  
> Locate the first divergence.  
> Test observer variables against target, context, measurement, representation, time, noise, and error.  
> Keep the observer in the model only when the observer improves discrimination.**

In its smallest form:

```text
A OBSERVES X

B OBSERVES Y

WHAT STAYED THE SAME?

WHERE DID X AND Y
BEGIN TO DIFFER?

WHAT VARIABLE
BEST EXPLAINS THAT DIFFERENCE?
```

The Comparative Observer Test does not assume the observer is the answer.

**It gives the observer a fair chance to prove whether it belongs in the explanation.**


Main writing choice: I made first divergence the central experimental target. Instead of treating the final disagreement as one block, the protocol traces the path from target → access → observation → representation → interpretation → hypothesis → conclusion and asks exactly where the two observer paths separate.
<img width="1194" height="672" alt="Triadic_Re-Ignition_experiments_index_" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e53d94fc-9bbb-4e9e-9e95-b9e064ee04e0" />

# Experiments

> **A framework becomes more useful when its claims can be translated into observations, comparisons, discriminators, and failure conditions.**

The Experiments branch of Triadic Re-Ignition turns exploratory concepts into structured investigations.

Its purpose is not to prove the framework.

Its purpose is to ask:

```text
What can be observed?

What can be compared?

What can be repeated?

What can be measured?

What would distinguish
competing explanations?

What would make us
revise the model?
```

The branch begins with clean observation and progressively adds comparison, cue testing, transfer, stabilization, and student simulation.

---

## Context

```text
RTT: 1
coherence: declared
drift: bounded
paradox: structural
```

**Module:** Triadic Re-Ignition  
**Domain:** Experiments  
**Status:** Active exploratory experimental layer

---

# Experimental Posture

The core experimental posture is:

```text
OBSERVATION
     ↓
CAPTURE
     ↓
OPERATIONALIZE
     ↓
COMPARE
     ↓
GENERATE ALTERNATIVES
     ↓
DEFINE DISCRIMINATORS
     ↓
TEST
     ↓
REVISE
```

The purpose is not to protect the original interpretation.

The purpose is to determine:

```text
what survives contact
with comparison and testing
```

---

# Core Experimental Rule

Every experimental document in this branch should preserve the distinction:

```text
WHAT HAPPENED
       ≠
WHAT EXPLAINS IT
```

A result may support:

```text
a relationship
```

without supporting:

```text
the preferred mechanism
```

A mechanism may eventually become well supported.

It must earn that status through evidence.

---

# Experimental Architecture

The current Experiments branch contains four primary artifacts:

```text
OBSERVATION PROTOCOL
        ↓
How do we capture cleanly?

COMPARATIVE OBSERVER TEST
        ↓
What changes across observers,
states, contexts, or forms?

RESONANCE RECALL TEST
        ↓
What changes after
a defined cue or trigger?

STUDENT SIMULATION
        ↓
What changes when students
reason through the same problem
under different analytical regimes?
```

Together:

```text
CAPTURE
   ↓
COMPARE
   ↓
TRIGGER
   ↓
TEST ACCESS
   ↓
TRANSFER
   ↓
REVISIT
   ↓
TEACH / SIMULATE
```

---

# 1. Observation Protocol

**File:** `./observation-protocol.md`

The Observation Protocol is the experimental root of the branch.

Its core sequence is:

```text
OBSERVE
   ↓
CAPTURE
   ↓
ANCHOR
   ↓
LOCATE THE OBSERVER
   ↓
SEPARATE INTERPRETATION
   ↓
IDENTIFY INVARIANTS
   ↓
GENERATE ALTERNATIVES
   ↓
DEFINE DISCRIMINATORS
   ↓
TEST
   ↓
REVISIT
```

The permanent boundary is:

```text
CAPTURE
    ≠
PROOF
```

---

# Why Observation Comes First

If the original observation is not preserved, later testing may accidentally test:

```text
the story about the event
```

rather than:

```text
the event as originally observed
```

Therefore the protocol attempts to preserve:

```text
prior state

trigger

first signal

recognition

first representation

initial interpretation

later interpretation
```

as separate layers where possible.

---

# Observation Categories

Experimental records should identify the relevant access channel.

```text
DIRECT OBSERVATION

MEASUREMENT

MEMORY REPORT

EXTERNAL RECORD

OTHER OBSERVER REPORT

MODEL OUTPUT

INFERENCE
```

These categories may interact.

They should not be silently treated as equivalent.

---

# Minimum Supported Claim

Every experiment should attempt to end with:

```text
MINIMUM SUPPORTED CLAIM
```

This should be the smallest statement that:

```text
preserves the result

respects uncertainty

avoids unsupported mechanism

and survives current evidence
```

This is one of the branch's primary anti-drift tools.

---

# 2. Comparative Observer Test

**File:** `./comparative-observer-test.md`

The Comparative Observer Test examines differences across:

```text
observers

observer states

contexts

representations

positions

or times
```

Its basic structure is:

```text
TARGET S
    +
OBSERVER CONDITION A
    ↓
OBSERVATION A
```

compared with:

```text
TARGET S
    +
OBSERVER CONDITION B
    ↓
OBSERVATION B
```

---

# Comparative Question

The primary question is:

> **Where do the observations first begin to diverge?**

The test searches for:

```text
shared invariants

changed variables

first divergence

observer effects

representation effects

context effects

measurement effects

alternative explanations
```

The permanent boundary is:

```text
DIFFERENT OBSERVATIONS
        ≠
OBSERVER EFFECT PROVEN
```

---

# First Divergence

Rather than treating disagreement as one block:

```text
A ≠ B
```

trace:

```text
TARGET
  ↓
ACCESS
  ↓
OBSERVATION
  ↓
REPRESENTATION
  ↓
INTERPRETATION
  ↓
HYPOTHESIS
  ↓
CONCLUSION
```

Then mark:

```text
FIRST DIVERGENCE
```

This often tells us where the next experiment belongs.

---

# Triadic Comparison

When observations conflict:

```text
A
+
B
+
OBSERVER / CONDITIONS
```

replaces premature:

```text
A OR B
```

But the third position does not require synthesis.

Possible results remain:

```text
A survives

B survives

both apply under
different conditions

both require revision

both fail

unknown
```

---

# 3. Resonance Recall Test

**File:** `./resonance-recall-test.md`

The Resonance Recall Test examines whether a defined cue is associated with renewed access to a previously encountered relationship.

Its working sequence is:

```text
EARLIER EXPOSURE
      ↓
EVIDENCE OF EARLIER ACCESS
      ↓
REDUCED BASELINE ACCESS
      ↓
CUE
      ↓
FIRST SIGNAL
      ↓
RECOGNITION
      ↓
RECALL
      ↓
RECONSTRUCTION
      ↓
FUNCTION
      ↓
TRANSFER
      ↓
DELAYED RETEST
```

---

# Recall-Test Question

The primary question is:

> **Does a structurally related cue change access to a previously encountered relationship?**

The test separately measures:

```text
familiarity

recognition

free recall

reconstruction

functional use

transfer

delayed stability
```

These outcomes should not automatically be collapsed.

---

# Recall-Test Boundaries

The permanent distinctions include:

```text
CUE
    ≠
PROVEN CAUSE
```

```text
FAMILIARITY
    ≠
ACCURACY
```

```text
RECOGNITION
    ≠
RECALL
```

```text
RECALL
    ≠
RECONSTRUCTION
```

```text
CONTINUITY
    ≠
IDENTITY
```

```text
STABILIZATION
    ≠
TRUTH
```

These distinctions allow a positive result to remain informative without becoming larger than the evidence.

---

# Cue Conditions

Potential comparisons include:

```text
RELATED CUE

SURFACE-SIMILAR CUE

UNRELATED CUE

NO-CUE REPETITION
```

The purpose is to ask whether changed access follows:

```text
shared structure
```

rather than merely:

```text
repetition

attention

surface familiarity

or expectation
```

---

# Cross-Form Testing

A strong experimental pattern is:

```text
Earlier Exposure
    =
Form A

Cue
    =
Form B

Transfer Test
    =
Form C
```

Then ask:

```text
What relationship survives
across all three forms?
```

A surviving relationship becomes a candidate structural invariant.

---

# 4. Student Simulation

**File:** `./student-simulation.md`

The Student Simulation applies the experimental discipline to reasoning itself.

Instead of teaching:

```text
the correct Triadic answer
```

students preserve several analytical passes.

```text
PASS 1
Initial Analysis

        ↓

PASS 2
Observer-Aware Analysis

        ↓

PASS 3
Triadic Analysis

        ↓

COMPARE
```

The change between passes becomes part of the experiment.

---

# Student-Simulation Question

The primary question is:

> **Does explicitly introducing observer, context, invariant, paradox, alternative hypotheses, and discriminators change how students analyze an ambiguous problem?**

Possible outcomes include:

```text
stronger analysis

same conclusion with
better justification

more useful uncertainty

unnecessary complexity

no meaningful difference
```

All are valid.

---

# Framework Is Not the Answer Key

The Student Simulation preserves:

```text
framework
    =
reasoning instrument
```

not:

```text
framework
    =
preferred conclusion
```

A student may complete the triadic analysis and conclude:

```text
the original simple
explanation still fits best
```

That is a successful result if the reasoning supports it.

---

# The Experimental Spine

The four artifacts can be connected as:

```text
OBSERVATION PROTOCOL
        ↓
preserve the event

COMPARATIVE OBSERVER TEST
        ↓
compare observation conditions

RESONANCE RECALL TEST
        ↓
manipulate cue conditions
and test renewed access

STUDENT SIMULATION
        ↓
compare reasoning regimes
```

The sequence moves from:

```text
DESCRIPTION
```

toward:

```text
COMPARISON
```

toward:

```text
INTERVENTION
```

toward:

```text
EDUCATIONAL APPLICATION
```

---

# Experimental Claim Ladder

Experimental claims should be separated by strength.

### Level 1: Observation

```text
A result occurred.
```

### Level 2: Association

```text
The result occurred alongside
a defined condition.
```

### Level 3: Reproducible Difference

```text
Changing a defined condition
systematically changed the result.
```

### Level 4: Structural Relationship

```text
A stable invariant or dependency
connects the conditions and results.
```

### Level 5: Operational Model

```text
A defined model predicts
the observed relationship.
```

### Level 6: Mechanism

```text
A defined process explains
why the relationship occurs.
```

### Level 7: General Mechanism

```text
The process generalizes across
relevant observers, targets,
and conditions.
```

### Level 8: Physical Principle

```text
The mechanism describes
a general physical process.
```

### Level 9: Ontological Claim

```text
The process reveals the
underlying nature of reality.
```

Experimental work should not skip levels merely because a result is compelling.

---

# Experimental Guardrails

The branch carries several permanent boundaries.

```text
OBSERVATION
    ≠
INTERPRETATION
```

```text
TRIGGER
    ≠
CAUSE
```

```text
RESONANCE
    ≠
CAUSATION
```

```text
RECOGNITION
    ≠
VERIFICATION
```

```text
OBSERVER DIFFERENCE
    ≠
OBSERVER EFFECT PROVEN
```

```text
AGREEMENT
    ≠
TRUTH
```

```text
DISAGREEMENT
    ≠
RELATIVITY
```

```text
REPRESENTATION
    ≠
COMPLETE STRUCTURE
```

```text
FORMLESS
    ≠
HIDDEN REALITY PROVEN
```

```text
STABILIZATION
    ≠
TRUTH
```

---

# Experimental Variables

A Triadic Re-Ignition experiment may involve variables from several layers.

```text
TARGET VARIABLES

What is being observed?
```

```text
OBSERVER VARIABLES

Who or what is observing,
and under what conditions?
```

```text
CONTEXT VARIABLES

What surrounding conditions
may matter?
```

```text
REPRESENTATION VARIABLES

How is the target represented?
```

```text
TEMPORAL VARIABLES

When does the observation
occur in the sequence?
```

```text
TRIGGER VARIABLES

What cue or condition changes?
```

```text
RESPONSE VARIABLES

What observation or performance
is measured?
```

The relevant variables depend on the hypothesis.

---

# Operationalization

A concept becomes experimentally useful when it can be translated into something observable.

For example:

```text
"Recognition"
```

might be operationalized as:

```text
correct identification
of a defined relationship
```

while:

```text
"Stabilization"
```

might be operationalized as:

```text
successful delayed
or cross-form access
under specified conditions
```

The operational definition must be stated explicitly.

---

# Operationalization Is Not Identity

An operational measure does not become the complete meaning of the concept.

For example:

```text
Recognition Measure
    =
correct selection
```

does not mean:

```text
recognition itself
    =
correct selection
in every context
```

The measure is a testing instrument.

Its scope should remain visible.

---

# Baseline

Whenever possible, establish a baseline.

```text
BASELINE
    ↓
INTERVENTION / CONDITION
    ↓
POST-CONDITION
```

The baseline helps determine whether:

```text
anything changed
```

But baseline measurement itself may affect the observer.

This should be documented.

---

# Controls

Useful comparison conditions may include:

```text
no-intervention

unrelated cue

surface-similar cue

alternative representation

different observer condition

different context

repetition-only condition
```

Controls should be selected to distinguish the actual hypotheses under investigation.

There is no universal control condition.

---

# Confounds

Potential confounding variables may include:

```text
prior exposure

training

expectation

task repetition

representation

context

available information

target change

timing

measurement method
```

The experiment should record important confounds rather than pretending perfect control.

---

# First Signal

Some experiments may capture the earliest reported signal before a full interpretation forms.

```text
TRIGGER
   ↓
FIRST SIGNAL
   ↓
RECOGNITION
   ↓
INTERPRETATION
```

Possible first signals include:

```text
familiarity

salience

unexpected correspondence

contradiction

partial recognition
```

The first signal is data.

It is not proof of mechanism.

---

# Recognition

Recognition should be distinguished from:

```text
familiarity

confidence

recall

reconstruction

functional use
```

A participant may score differently across all five.

That pattern may be more informative than a single combined score.

---

# Reintegration

Experimental reintegration may be indicated when the participant can:

```text
explain a relationship

revise a previous model

connect the relationship
to current knowledge

or use it coherently
```

The exact criterion should be defined by the protocol.

---

# Stabilization

Stabilization may be tested through:

```text
repeated access

delayed retest

cross-form transfer

new-context performance

independent application

cross-observer recognition
```

Again:

```text
stable
    ≠
true
```

Stability makes further investigation easier.

---

# Invariants

Invariant detection is one of the branch's central tools.

```text
Condition A ──┐
              │
Condition B ──┼── Invariant R?
              │
Condition C ──┘
```

The invariant may be:

```text
relationship

ordering

function

transformation

measurement

prediction

error pattern
```

The invariant should be stated as precisely as practical.

---

# Differences

Experiments must also preserve changed components.

```text
BEFORE
│
├── invariant A
└── variable X

AFTER
│
├── invariant A
└── variable Y
```

The experiment then asks:

```text
What best explains X → Y?
```

This is more discriminative than:

```text
"Something changed."
```

---

# Divergence Point

When two paths differ:

```text
A → B → C → D
        │
        └── X → Y
```

identify:

```text
the first meaningful divergence
```

Possible locations include:

```text
access

observation

measurement

memory

representation

interpretation

hypothesis

conclusion
```

The divergence point often identifies the next variable to test.

---

# Alternative Hypotheses

The branch should preserve at least one meaningful competing explanation where practical.

A general structure is:

```text
OBSERVATION
   ├── H1
   ├── H2
   ├── H3
   └── UNKNOWN
```

Alternatives should be relevant.

The goal is not endless hypothesis generation.

---

# Discriminator

A discriminator asks:

```text
What result would favor
H1 over H2?
```

This is one of the strongest transitions from conceptual reasoning into experimental design.

Without a discriminator:

```text
two explanations
```

may remain only:

```text
two stories
```

---

# Failure Condition

Every preferred hypothesis should attempt to specify:

```text
What would make this
less likely?
```

If no failure condition exists yet:

```text
NOT YET OPERATIONALIZED
```

is more honest than inventing one.

---

# Unknown

`UNKNOWN` remains an explicit experimental result.

Use it when:

```text
data are insufficient

results conflict

mechanism is unresolved

a variable cannot be isolated

or multiple hypotheses
remain viable
```

Unknown is not failed research.

It marks the current boundary.

---

# Null Results

A null result may be:

```text
no cue effect

no observer effect

no cross-form invariant

no delayed stability

no change after
triadic prompting
```

These results should be preserved.

They help narrow the model.

---

# Negative Results

A result may directly challenge a preferred claim.

For example:

```text
related cue performs worse
than unrelated cue
```

or:

```text
observer-condition change
does not alter observation
```

or:

```text
relationship disappears
under alternative form
```

Such results are valuable.

They should not be reframed automatically as hidden confirmation.

---

# Failed Hypotheses

When a hypothesis fails:

```text
PRESERVE IT
```

Record:

```text
what it predicted

what occurred

why the prediction failed

what model replaced it
```

Failed hypotheses improve the revision history.

---

# Revision History

Experimental models may progress:

```text
MODEL v1
    ↓
Observation
    ↓
MODEL v2
    ↓
Experiment
    ↓
MODEL v3
```

Preserve the transitions.

The history may reveal:

```text
where drift occurred

where assumptions failed

which invariants survived
```

---

# Experimental Drift

Experiments can drift too.

A common pattern is:

```text
result observed
      ↓
preferred explanation
      ↓
framework vocabulary added
      ↓
result interpreted as confirmation
```

The bounded sequence is:

```text
result observed
      ↓
minimum supported claim
      ↓
compare hypotheses
      ↓
define discriminator
      ↓
test
      ↓
revise
```

---

# Confirmation Drift

Because Triadic Re-Ignition provides rich vocabulary, almost any result could potentially be described using:

```text
observer

resonance

form

drift

paradox

projection

regime
```

This creates a special danger.

The vocabulary must not become:

```text
automatic confirmation machinery
```

Instead ask:

```text
Did the concept predict anything?

Did it improve discrimination?

Could the result have been
explained without it?
```

---

# Framework Falsifiability

Triadic Re-Ignition should remain capable of being narrowed.

For example:

```text
Resonance Before Form
```

should weaken if:

```text
stable representation
consistently precedes recognition
```

A proposed observer effect should weaken if:

```text
varying observer condition
does not change results
```

A trigger hypothesis should weaken if:

```text
relevant controls perform equally
```

A cross-form structural claim should weaken if:

```text
the relationship disappears
under representation change
```

The framework should learn from these results.

---

# Simpler Models

Experiments should compare:

```text
TRIADIC MODEL
```

with:

```text
SIMPLER MODEL
```

when possible.

Ask:

```text
Does the additional structure
explain something the simpler
model cannot?

Does it improve prediction?

Does it identify a new
discriminator?

Does it reduce unexplained variance?
```

If not:

```text
prefer the simpler model
for that case
```

The framework does not need to be present in every explanation.

---

# Observer-Aware Without Observer Inflation

The Experiments branch keeps observer variables available.

It does not assume:

```text
the observer causes
the phenomenon
```

The relevant question is:

```text
Does including observer condition
improve the model?
```

If not:

```text
remove or reduce
the observer variable
```

---

# Representation-Aware Without Form Inflation

Likewise, representation may matter.

But:

```text
representation changes
      ≠
underlying structure changes
```

and:

```text
representation effects
      ≠
all structure is representation
```

The experiment should distinguish these levels where possible.

---

# Time-Aware Without Timeline Inflation

Temporal experiments should separate:

```text
PHYSICAL TIME

LOCAL TIMELINE

RESONANCE TIME

TIMELINE PROJECTION
```

A changed temporal representation does not automatically establish:

```text
changed physical history
```

or:

```text
multiple physical timelines
```

Those are stronger hypotheses.

---

# Formless-Aware Without Hidden-Reality Inflation

An unresolved relationship may be marked:

```text
FORMLESS
```

within the module's operational vocabulary.

But:

```text
FORMLESS
    =
representation boundary
```

not:

```text
hidden reality verified
```

Experiments should attempt to move:

```text
unresolved
```

toward:

```text
operationalized
```

rather than merely renaming the unknown.

---

# Universe-as-Operator Experimental Boundary

If an experiment invokes:

```text
Universe as Operator
```

it should specify:

```text
what broader condition
is being modeled

what the operator acts on

what transformation is expected

what invariant should survive

what simpler model competes
```

Otherwise the concept remains too broad to test.

---

# Experimental Workflow

A general Re-Ignition experiment can use:

```text
1. DEFINE QUESTION

2. DEFINE TARGET

3. DEFINE OBSERVER

4. DEFINE VARIABLES

5. DEFINE BASELINE

6. CAPTURE PRIOR STATE

7. RUN CONDITION

8. CAPTURE FIRST SIGNAL

9. MEASURE RESPONSE

10. SEPARATE INTERPRETATION

11. IDENTIFY INVARIANTS

12. IDENTIFY DIFFERENCES

13. GENERATE ALTERNATIVES

14. DEFINE DISCRIMINATOR

15. DEFINE FAILURE CONDITION

16. REPEAT / TRANSFER / DELAY

17. COMPARE

18. WRITE MINIMUM SUPPORTED CLAIM

19. PRESERVE UNKNOWN

20. REVISE MODEL
```

Not every experiment requires every step.

The sequence can be adapted to the question.

---

# Experimental Status

A study or protocol may be labeled:

```text
PROPOSED
```

```text
PILOT
```

```text
UNDER TEST
```

```text
REPEATED
```

```text
PARTIALLY SUPPORTED
```

```text
NOT SUPPORTED
```

```text
INCONCLUSIVE
```

```text
REVISED
```

Status should describe the experiment or result, not imply canonical truth.

---

# Evidence Status

Individual claims may use:

```text
OBSERVED

REPORTED

MEASURED

INFERRED

HYPOTHESIZED

SUPPORTED

NOT SUPPORTED

UNKNOWN
```

This makes claim state visible across documents.

---

# Student Research Posture

Students using this branch should be encouraged to say:

```text
"I don't know yet."
```

They should also be encouraged to say:

```text
"My first explanation
still fits best."
```

or:

```text
"The Triadic model
did not add anything useful."
```

These are legitimate research outcomes.

---

# AI-Assisted Experimentation

AI systems may assist with:

```text
scenario generation

alternative hypotheses

claim classification

comparison structure

question generation

drift checking

experimental brainstorming
```

But:

```text
AI output
    ≠
experimental observation
```

AI-generated hypotheses remain hypotheses.

AI-generated interpretations must not be silently inserted into participant data.

---

# AI and Observer Effects

If an AI system interacts with a participant before or during testing, it may alter:

```text
context

expectation

representation

available information

observer state
```

Therefore AI involvement should be documented as part of the experimental condition when relevant.

---

# Human and AI Comparison

A future experiment may compare:

```text
human observer

AI model

human + AI observer system
```

But these should not be presumed equivalent observer types.

The comparison would require its own operational definitions.

---

# Ethical Boundary

Experiments in this branch are intended for:

```text
education

reasoning research

low-stakes pattern analysis

model comparison

and exploratory framework testing
```

They should not be used as unvalidated procedures for:

```text
clinical diagnosis

forensic memory recovery

legal proof

mental-health classification

or high-stakes decision making
```

Those applications require validated domain-specific methods.

---

# Experimental Success

An experiment succeeds when it produces useful discrimination.

That may mean:

```text
supporting a hypothesis
```

or:

```text
weakening a hypothesis
```

or:

```text
rejecting a hypothesis
```

or:

```text
revealing a confound
```

or:

```text
showing that
the question is not
yet operationalized
```

All can improve the framework.

---

# What the Branch Should Learn

The Experiments branch should gradually determine:

```text
which Re-Ignition concepts
are operationally useful

which remain metaphors

which require revision

which duplicate existing concepts

which generate predictions

which improve discrimination

and which should be removed
```

A framework that cannot lose unnecessary parts cannot learn effectively from experiment.

---

# Research Questions

1. Which Re-Ignition concepts can be operationalized reliably?

2. Which concepts improve discrimination beyond ordinary models?

3. Can renewed access be separated from relearning?

4. Can reconstruction be distinguished from recall?

5. Can resonance be separated from familiarity and salience?

6. Can recognition be shown to precede stable form?

7. Can observer effects be reproduced?

8. Can representation effects be separated from observer effects?

9. Can cross-form invariants be identified reliably?

10. Can timeline revision be separated cleanly from physical chronology?

11. Can apparent multiplicity be localized to a specific layer?

12. Does the Minimum Supported Claim reduce interpretive drift?

13. Does paradox preservation improve later discrimination?

14. Does requiring alternative hypotheses reduce narrative lock?

15. Does defining failure conditions improve model revision?

16. Do Triadic prompts improve student reasoning?

17. When do Triadic prompts add unnecessary complexity?

18. Can experiments be reproduced without Triadic terminology?

19. Which module concepts should be abandoned if they fail repeatedly?

20. What evidence would justify stronger formal or mechanistic models?

---

# Working Summary

The Experiments branch asks Triadic Re-Ignition to do something philosophy alone cannot do:

```text
RISK BEING WRONG
```

Its architecture is:

```text
OBSERVATION PROTOCOL
        ↓
capture cleanly

COMPARATIVE OBSERVER TEST
        ↓
compare conditions

RESONANCE RECALL TEST
        ↓
manipulate cues
and measure access

STUDENT SIMULATION
        ↓
compare reasoning regimes
```

The experimental sequence is:

```text
OBSERVE
   ↓
OPERATIONALIZE
   ↓
BASELINE
   ↓
COMPARE
   ↓
INTERVENE
   ↓
MEASURE
   ↓
FIND INVARIANTS
   ↓
LOCATE DIVERGENCE
   ↓
GENERATE ALTERNATIVES
   ↓
DEFINE DISCRIMINATORS
   ↓
TEST
   ↓
REPEAT
   ↓
REVISE
```

The branch keeps several permanent boundaries:

```text
CAPTURE
    ≠
PROOF

TRIGGER
    ≠
CAUSE

RESONANCE
    ≠
CAUSATION

RECOGNITION
    ≠
VERIFICATION

OBSERVER DIFFERENCE
    ≠
OBSERVER EFFECT PROVEN

AGREEMENT
    ≠
TRUTH

CONTINUITY
    ≠
IDENTITY

REPRESENTATION
    ≠
COMPLETE STRUCTURE

STABILIZATION
    ≠
TRUTH
```

The guiding discipline is:

> **Do not design experiments to make Re-Ignition win.  
> Design experiments that give competing explanations a fair chance to win.  
> Preserve baselines.  
> Hold variables stable where practical.  
> Record confounds where they cannot be controlled.  
> Search for invariants.  
> Locate divergence.  
> Define failure before certainty.  
> Keep null and negative results.  
> Remove concepts that repeatedly fail to improve the model.**

In its smallest form:

```text
WHAT DID WE OBSERVE?
        ↓
WHAT CHANGED?
        ↓
WHAT STAYED THE SAME?
        ↓
WHAT ELSE EXPLAINS IT?
        ↓
WHAT RESULT WOULD
SEPARATE THE MODELS?
        ↓
TEST
```

The Experiments branch is not where Triadic Re-Ignition goes to prove itself.

**It is where Triadic Re-Ignition gives the evidence permission to change it.**


Main writing choice: I made the branch explicitly framework-falsifiable. experiments/ now has a clear progression of capture → compare → intervene → transfer → teach, while preserving null results, negative results, simpler models, and even the possibility that a Triadic operator adds no useful discrimination in a given case.

# Observation Protocol

> **Preserve what happened before deciding what it means.**

The Observation Protocol provides the baseline experimental method for Triadic Re-Ignition.

Its purpose is to preserve an observation in a form that can later support:

```text
comparison

observer analysis

timeline reconstruction

invariant detection

alternative hypotheses

experimental testing

and revision
```

The core sequence is:

```text
OBSERVE
   ↓
CAPTURE
   ↓
ANCHOR
   ↓
LOCATE THE OBSERVER
   ↓
SEPARATE INTERPRETATION
   ↓
IDENTIFY INVARIANTS
   ↓
GENERATE ALTERNATIVES
   ↓
DEFINE DISCRIMINATORS
   ↓
TEST
   ↓
REVISE
```

The protocol does not require the observer to suppress interpretation.

It requires interpretation to remain distinguishable from the observation that produced it.

---

## Context

```text
RTT: 1
coherence: declared
drift: bounded
paradox: structural
```

**Module:** Triadic Re-Ignition  
**Domain:** Experiments  
**Artifact:** Observation Protocol  
**Status:** Exploratory baseline protocol

---

# Core Principle

The simplest distinction is:

```text
WHAT HAPPENED
       ≠
WHAT I THINK IT MEANS
```

Both matter.

But they occupy different layers.

A useful observation record therefore preserves:

```text
OBSERVATION
     ↓
What happened?

INTERPRETATION
     ↓
What might it mean?

HYPOTHESIS
     ↓
What could explain it?

TEST
     ↓
What could distinguish
the explanations?
```

This separation provides the foundation for later analysis.

---

# Why Capture Comes First

Observation can be reorganized very quickly by interpretation.

A possible sequence is:

```text
EVENT
  ↓
FIRST SIGNAL
  ↓
RECOGNITION
  ↓
INTERPRETATION
  ↓
STORY
```

After the story stabilizes, it may become difficult to remember:

```text
what appeared first
```

versus:

```text
what was added afterward
```

The protocol therefore prioritizes early capture.

---

# Capture Is Not Proof

A captured observation is:

```text
a preserved report
```

It is not automatically:

```text
verified evidence

causal evidence

mechanistic evidence

or proof of ontology
```

Therefore:

```text
CAPTURE
    ≠
VERIFICATION
```

Capture protects the observation from being lost.

Later stages evaluate what the observation supports.

---

# Observation Categories

An observation should identify its access channel where possible.

Possible categories include:

```text
DIRECT OBSERVATION

MEASUREMENT

MEMORY REPORT

EXTERNAL RECORD

OTHER OBSERVER REPORT

MODEL OUTPUT

INFERENCE
```

These may provide different evidence properties.

They should not automatically be treated as interchangeable.

---

# Direct Observation

A direct observation records what the observer reports perceiving or detecting in the present interaction.

Example structure:

```text
"I observed X."
```

Then separately:

```text
"I interpreted X as Y."
```

This preserves the difference between event and explanation.

---

# Measurement

A measurement includes a defined instrument, scale, procedure, or recorded value.

Capture:

```text
what was measured

how it was represented

what instrument or method was used

what conditions were present
```

Do not silently replace:

```text
measured result
```

with:

```text
interpretation of measured result
```

---

# Memory Report

A memory report should be labeled as memory.

```text
MEMORY REPORT

"I remember X."
```

This should remain distinguishable from:

```text
EXTERNAL RECORD

"Document Y records X."
```

Agreement between them may be informative.

Disagreement may also be informative.

---

# External Record

External records may include:

```text
documents

notes

recordings

saved artifacts

measurements

previous responses

logs
```

Preserve the original record when practical rather than relying only on later summary.

---

# Other Observer Report

If another observer supplies information, capture:

```text
what they reported

when they reported it

what they directly observed

what they inferred
```

Do not silently convert another person's interpretation into direct observation.

---

# Model Output

A model may produce:

```text
prediction

classification

simulation result

generated representation
```

Model output should remain labeled as:

```text
MODEL OUTPUT
```

rather than:

```text
OBSERVED REALITY
```

unless external observation independently establishes correspondence.

---

# Inference

Inference is necessary.

But it should be visible.

```text
OBSERVATION

A
```

```text
OBSERVATION

B
```

```text
INFERENCE

A and B may be related.
```

Then:

```text
HYPOTHESIS

Relationship R explains A and B.
```

This preserves the reasoning chain.

---

# Immediate Capture

When an observation appears significant, record the smallest useful sequence.

```text
WHAT HAPPENED?

WHAT HAPPENED IMMEDIATELY BEFORE?

WHAT DID I NOTICE FIRST?

WHAT BECAME RECOGNIZABLE?

WHAT DID I THINK IT MEANT?
```

Do not wait for a complete theory.

Incomplete early capture may be more useful than polished retrospective narrative.

---

# The First Signal

Triadic Re-Ignition gives special attention to:

```text
FIRST SIGNAL
```

This may be:

```text
familiarity

salience

unexpected correspondence

contradiction

pattern recognition

a question

a representation failure
```

The first signal is not automatically meaningful.

But preserving it helps reconstruct the event sequence.

---

# Observation Versus Recognition

The observer may notice something before explicitly identifying it.

```text
OBSERVATION
    ↓
FIRST SIGNAL
    ↓
RESONANCE
    ↓
RECOGNITION
```

These stages may occur rapidly.

The protocol should preserve their order when the observer can report it.

---

# Recognition Versus Explanation

A Recognition Event may be:

```text
"There it is."
```

The explanation may follow:

```text
"This must mean..."
```

Therefore:

```text
RECOGNITION
    ≠
EXPLANATION
```

The protocol records both.

It does not merge them.

---

# Temporal Anchor

Every observation should be temporally anchored as precisely as the available evidence permits.

Record:

```text
event order

known timestamps

relative sequence

defined intervals
```

Do not invent precision that was not available.

If exact timing is unknown:

```text
UNKNOWN
```

is valid.

---

# Event Sequence

A minimal sequence may be:

```text
E₁
 ↓
E₂
 ↓
E₃
 ↓
OBSERVATION
```

For Re-Ignition:

```text
PRIOR STATE
    ↓
TRIGGER
    ↓
FIRST SIGNAL
    ↓
RECOGNITION
    ↓
INTERPRETATION
```

The sequence itself may later help distinguish competing explanations.

---

# Relative Timing

When exact timing is unavailable, preserve relative order.

For example:

```text
The cue appeared first.

Recognition occurred afterward.

The explanation came later.
```

This is more useful than assigning unsupported timestamps.

---

# Observer Location

Every observation occurs from a position.

Record:

```text
observer

physical position

temporal position

available information

context

representation

relevant prior knowledge
```

Only variables relevant to the task need to be captured.

The objective is not to profile the observer.

It is to preserve observational conditions.

---

# Local Observer Record

A useful observer record is:

```text
OBSERVER

Who or what observed?
```

```text
POSITION

From where?
```

```text
ACCESS

What information was available?
```

```text
CONTEXT

Under what conditions?
```

```text
FORM

How was the relationship represented?
```

This makes later comparison easier.

---

# Observer State

Observer state may include relevant variables such as:

```text
knowledge

attention

prior exposure

memory access

current context

representation

expectation
```

These should be recorded when relevant.

They should not be inferred from unrelated personal characteristics.

---

# Observer Transition

If observation changes:

```text
Observer State A
        ↓
Observation A
```

then:

```text
Observer State B
        ↓
Observation B
```

record:

```text
what changed between A and B
```

rather than assuming the external structure changed.

---

# Locality

The protocol treats observation as local.

```text
LOCAL
    ≠
FALSE
```

and:

```text
LOCAL
    ≠
COMPLETE
```

The observer reports what is accessible from the current position.

Broader claims require additional evidence.

---

# Context

Context can alter:

```text
attention

interpretation

access

cue effectiveness

representation

measurement
```

Record relevant context before deciding whether it matters.

Possible context variables include:

```text
task

environment

instructions

available materials

preceding events

representation used
```

---

# Representation

Record how the observation is being represented.

Possible forms include:

```text
prose

diagram

timeline

equation

table

category

model

image

symbol
```

Representation matters because one form may expose relationships another form hides.

---

# First Form

For Re-Ignition events, preserve the earliest usable representation where possible.

```text
FIRST SIGNAL
    ↓
RECOGNITION
    ↓
FIRST FORM
```

Later representations may be more refined.

The differences between them may contain useful evidence about interpretation and reintegration.

---

# Alternative Form

After preserving the first form, attempt another representation.

```text
FORM A
   ↓
FORM B
```

Then ask:

```text
What changed?

What remained invariant?

What disappeared?

What became visible?
```

This can help distinguish structural relationships from representation-specific effects.

---

# Form / Formless Boundary

The protocol may record:

```text
WHAT IS CURRENTLY REPRESENTABLE
```

and:

```text
WHAT REMAINS UNRESOLVED
```

The unresolved side should not automatically be labeled:

```text
hidden structure
```

The appropriate status may simply be:

```text
UNKNOWN
```

---

# Raw Observation Layer

The raw observation layer should contain the smallest practical description of what occurred.

For example:

```text
"After seeing diagram X,
I recognized a similarity
between A and B."
```

Avoid immediately adding:

```text
because

therefore

must mean

proves

shows the mechanism
```

Those belong downstream.

---

# Interpretation Layer

Interpretation asks:

```text
What do I currently think
the observation means?
```

The interpretation may be:

```text
strong

weak

tentative

multiple

or absent
```

A valid entry is:

```text
UNKNOWN
```

---

# Hypothesis Layer

A hypothesis proposes an explanation.

```text
OBSERVATION
     ↓
INTERPRETATION
     ↓
HYPOTHESIS
```

Examples:

```text
H1
memory retrieval

H2
reconstruction

H3
representation effect

H4
context effect

H5
new synthesis

H6
measurement error

H7
unknown
```

The set should fit the observation rather than being mechanically reused.

---

# Alternative Hypothesis

Require at least one meaningful alternative when a preferred explanation exists.

This prevents:

```text
first explanation
      ↓
only explanation
      ↓
certainty
```

The purpose is not to generate endless possibilities.

It is to keep comparison alive.

---

# Minimum-Claim Layer

After describing the observation, write the smallest statement clearly supported by it.

Example experience:

```text
"I accessed another timeline."
```

Minimum observational claim:

```text
"I experienced a temporal
representation that appeared
inconsistent with my previous
timeline model."
```

Then preserve:

```text
another timeline
```

as a hypothesis if relevant.

---

# Claim Ladder

Statements should be classified by level.

```text
LEVEL 1
OBSERVATION
```

```text
LEVEL 2
RELATIONSHIP
```

```text
LEVEL 3
INTERPRETATION
```

```text
LEVEL 4
HYPOTHESIS
```

```text
LEVEL 5
MECHANISM
```

```text
LEVEL 6
GENERAL MECHANISM
```

```text
LEVEL 7
PHYSICAL PRINCIPLE
```

```text
LEVEL 8
ONTOLOGY
```

Not every investigation needs to climb the ladder.

---

# Claim Promotion

Movement upward should answer:

```text
What new evidence
justifies the stronger claim?
```

If no new evidence exists:

```text
do not promote the claim
```

A useful observation remains useful even if mechanism remains unknown.

---

# Invariants

When comparing observations, search for what remains stable.

```text
Observation A ──┐
                ├── Invariant R?
Observation B ──┘
```

Possible invariants include:

```text
event ordering

measurement

relationship

function

artifact

transformation

shared record

representation feature
```

Invariants help locate the layer at which change actually occurred.

---

# Difference Mapping

Also record:

```text
what changed
```

For example:

```text
STATE A
│
├── invariant X
├── invariant Y
└── variable P

STATE B
│
├── invariant X
├── invariant Y
└── variable Q
```

Then ask:

```text
What explains P → Q?
```

This produces a more precise research problem.

---

# Divergence Point

When two observations or models differ, locate the first meaningful divergence.

```text
A → B → C → D
        │
        └── X → Y
```

Ask whether divergence occurs in:

```text
physical event

memory

record

observer state

context

representation

measurement

interpretation
```

The divergence point often tells us where to investigate next.

---

# Paradox

If two observations conflict:

```text
A ≠ B
```

preserve the contradiction before resolving it.

```text
A
+
B
+
OBSERVER / CONTEXT
```

Then ask:

```text
What remains invariant?

What conditions differ?

What assumptions differ?

Could one observation be wrong?

Could both be incomplete?
```

Paradox is treated as a signal.

Not as proof of hidden structure.

---

# Paradox Record

A useful paradox entry is:

```text
MODEL / OBSERVATION A:
________________________________

MODEL / OBSERVATION B:
________________________________

EXACT CONTRADICTION:
________________________________

SHARED INVARIANT:
________________________________

DIFFERING CONDITION:
________________________________

CURRENT STATUS:
UNRESOLVED
```

This preserves the problem cleanly.

---

# Unknown

`UNKNOWN` is a first-class protocol state.

Use it when:

```text
timing is unknown

mechanism is unknown

observer variable is unknown

relationship is unclear

evidence is insufficient

or hypotheses remain tied
```

Do not fill unknown fields merely because the framework provides vocabulary.

---

# Missing Variable

If the current model does not explain an observation:

```text
OBSERVATION
      ↓
MODEL FAILURE
      ↓
MISSING VARIABLE?
```

Classify candidate missing variables broadly.

```text
system

observer

context

measurement

representation

time

noise

error

unknown
```

Do not jump directly to Hidden Observer.

---

# Hidden Observer Boundary

A Hidden Observer hypothesis becomes relevant only when:

```text
there is reason to suspect
a specific missing
observer-related dependency
```

It does not mean:

```text
hidden person

hidden intelligence

or unseen agent
```

The preferred outcome is to identify the variable and remove its hidden status.

---

# Re-Ignition Observation

When the observation involves renewed access, map it cautiously.

```text
EARLIER ACCESS
      ↓
REDUCED ACCESS
      ↓
TRIGGER?
      ↓
RESONANCE?
      ↓
RECOGNITION?
      ↓
REINTEGRATION?
      ↓
STABILIZATION?
```

Use:

```text
UNKNOWN
```

for stages not established by evidence.

Do not force the full sequence onto every event.

---

# Dormancy Check

Ask:

```text
Was the relationship
previously accessible?
```

Then:

```text
Is there evidence that
access later decreased?
```

Without both:

```text
Dormant Pattern
    =
not established
```

---

# Trigger Check

Ask:

```text
What happened immediately
before renewed salience?
```

Then preserve:

```text
trigger
    ≠
cause
```

The candidate trigger may later prove irrelevant.

---

# Resonance Check

Ask:

```text
What correspondence became salient?
```

Then specify:

```text
what exactly corresponds
```

If the relationship cannot yet be stated:

```text
candidate resonance
```

may remain provisional.

---

# Recognition Check

Ask:

```text
What became explicitly identifiable?
```

Then preserve:

```text
recognition
    ≠
verification
```

Subjective confidence should be recorded separately from accuracy.

---

# Reintegration Check

Ask:

```text
How did the recognized relationship
change the current model?
```

Possible outcomes include:

```text
direct fit

current model revised

recognized relationship revised

both revised

unresolved

rejected
```

---

# Stabilization Check

Ask:

```text
Can the relationship
be revisited later?

Does it survive another form?

Another context?

Another observer?

Challenge?
```

Then preserve:

```text
stabilization
    ≠
truth
```

---

# Local-Time Observation

For temporal events, separate several layers.

```text
PHYSICAL TIME

What event sequence
can be established?
```

```text
LOCAL TIMELINE

What chronology is accessible
to the observer?
```

```text
RESONANCE TIME

What appears structurally related
across chronological distance?
```

```text
TIMELINE PROJECTION

How might structure
become this representation?
```

Do not merge these layers automatically.

---

# Timeline Revision

If recognition changes interpretation of earlier events:

```text
OLD TIMELINE MODEL
        ↓
RECOGNITION
        ↓
NEW TIMELINE MODEL
```

record:

```text
what remained physically invariant
```

and:

```text
what changed representationally
```

The permanent boundary is:

```text
timeline revision
        ≠
timeline alteration
```

---

# Apparent Multiple Timelines

If an observation is experienced as:

```text
"another timeline"
```

preserve that report.

Then classify what is actually multiple.

```text
memory?

possibility?

representation?

observer state?

projection?

physical record?

physical timeline?

unknown?
```

The protocol does not rule physical multiplicity in or out.

It locates the current evidence level.

---

# Form Check

For every important claim, ask:

```text
What form is carrying
this interpretation?
```

Then:

```text
Can another form represent
the same observation?
```

Cross-form comparison can reveal representation dependence.

---

# Formless Check

If something remains difficult to represent:

```text
FORMLESS
```

may be used as a module-local boundary term.

But record:

```text
what exactly remains unresolved
```

rather than using Formless as the explanation.

---

# Universe-as-Operator Check

If a model invokes:

```text
Universe as Operator
```

require:

```text
What broader condition
is being represented?

What does the operator act on?

What transformation occurs?

What remains invariant?

Does the operator model add
anything beyond ordinary
boundary conditions?
```

Do not permit:

```text
operator
```

to silently become:

```text
agent
```

or:

```text
intent
```

---

# Observation Protocol Phases

The complete protocol can be divided into six phases.

```text
PHASE 1
CAPTURE
```

```text
PHASE 2
ANCHOR
```

```text
PHASE 3
SEPARATE
```

```text
PHASE 4
COMPARE
```

```text
PHASE 5
TEST
```

```text
PHASE 6
REVISIT
```

Each phase has a different purpose.

---

# Phase 1: Capture

Record:

```text
what happened

what happened immediately before

what appeared first

what became recognizable

what explanation appeared afterward
```

Preserve original wording where practical.

---

# Phase 2: Anchor

Record:

```text
event sequence

time

observer position

context

access channel

representation

external records
```

Use only the precision actually available.

---

# Phase 3: Separate

Distinguish:

```text
observation

memory

measurement

inference

interpretation

hypothesis

mechanism

ontology
```

This is the protocol's principal drift-control layer.

---

# Phase 4: Compare

Compare:

```text
earlier versus later

observer A versus observer B

form A versus form B

baseline versus post-trigger

prediction versus observation

model versus record
```

Search for:

```text
invariants

differences

divergence points
```

---

# Phase 5: Test

Ask:

```text
What can be repeated?

What can be measured?

What can be controlled?

What could discriminate
between hypotheses?

What result would weaken
the preferred explanation?
```

Do not require every observation to become experimentally testable immediately.

Operationalization may itself be the next research step.

---

# Phase 6: Revisit

Return after:

```text
more evidence

another observation

another representation

another observer

or a defined interval
```

Then ask:

```text
What still holds?

What changed?

What should be revised?

What remains unknown?
```

Preserve the revision history.

---

# Compact Observation Record

For rapid capture, use:

```text
WHAT HAPPENED?
________________________________

WHAT HAPPENED FIRST?
________________________________

WHAT WAS THE TRIGGER?
________________________________

WHAT DID I NOTICE?
________________________________

WHAT DID I RECOGNIZE?
________________________________

WHAT DO I THINK IT MEANS?
________________________________

WHAT ELSE COULD EXPLAIN IT?
________________________________

WHAT REMAINED INVARIANT?
________________________________

WHAT CHANGED?
________________________________

WHAT CAN I CHECK?
________________________________

WHAT REMAINS UNKNOWN?
________________________________
```

The compact form should be expandable into the full protocol later.

---

# Comparison Record

When two observations conflict:

```text
OBSERVATION A:
________________________________

OBSERVATION B:
________________________________

EXACT DIFFERENCE:
________________________________

OBSERVER A:
________________________________

OBSERVER B:
________________________________

CONTEXT A:
________________________________

CONTEXT B:
________________________________

FORM A:
________________________________

FORM B:
________________________________

SHARED INVARIANT:
________________________________

FIRST DIVERGENCE:
________________________________

POSSIBLE MISSING VARIABLE:
________________________________

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION:
________________________________

DISCRIMINATOR:
________________________________

CURRENT STATUS:
________________________________
```

---

# Observation Status

An observation may be classified as:

```text
CAPTURED
```

```text
ANCHORED
```

```text
UNDER COMPARISON
```

```text
OPERATIONALIZED
```

```text
UNDER TEST
```

```text
PARTIALLY SUPPORTED
```

```text
REVISED
```

```text
NOT SUPPORTED
```

```text
UNRESOLVED
```

Status describes the investigation.

It does not describe the observer's value or credibility.

---

# Evidence Status

Individual claims may also use:

```text
OBSERVED
```

```text
REPORTED
```

```text
MEASURED
```

```text
INFERRED
```

```text
HYPOTHESIZED
```

```text
SUPPORTED
```

```text
NOT SUPPORTED
```

```text
UNKNOWN
```

Do not convert these automatically into numerical probabilities unless the protocol defines how.

---

# Confidence

Observer confidence may be recorded.

Example:

```text
confidence:
low / medium / high
```

or through a defined numeric scale.

However:

```text
CONFIDENCE
    ≠
EVIDENCE STRENGTH
```

The scale should be specified if numerical ratings are used.

---

# False Recognition

If later evidence indicates the original recognition was mistaken:

```text
DO NOT DELETE
THE ORIGINAL RECORD
```

Instead preserve:

```text
ORIGINAL CAPTURE
      ↓
LATER CONTRADICTION
      ↓
REVISION
```

False recognition contains useful information about the transition.

---

# Failed Hypothesis

Likewise, if:

```text
H1
```

fails:

```text
preserve H1

record why it failed

record what evidence changed
```

Failed hypotheses improve the model when their failure conditions are visible.

---

# Revision History

A model may progress:

```text
v1
 ↓
new observation
 ↓
v2
 ↓
experiment
 ↓
v3
```

Preserve:

```text
what changed

why it changed

which invariants survived
```

Revision is expected.

It is not an error state.

---

# Drift Checks

Before promoting a claim, ask:

```text
Did observation become interpretation?

Did interpretation become mechanism?

Did mechanism become ontology?

Did trigger become cause?

Did recognition become verification?

Did local become global?

Did form become complete structure?

Did unresolved become hidden reality?

Did operator become agent?

Did stability become truth?
```

If yes:

```text
return to the
last supported layer
```

---

# Anti-Drift Ladder

Use:

```text
OBSERVATION
    ↓
RELATIONSHIP
    ↓
INTERPRETATION
    ↓
HYPOTHESIS
    ↓
TEST
    ↓
MECHANISM
    ↓
BROADER CLAIM
```

Each transition should be traceable.

---

# Observer Safety Check

Observer-aware analysis should not become:

```text
profiling the observer
```

or:

```text
pathologizing disagreement
```

The protocol focuses on:

```text
conditions relevant
to the observation
```

not unsupported assumptions about the observer's identity, motives, personality, or mental state.

---

# Personal Interpretation Boundary

For self-observation:

```text
"I experienced X."
```

is legitimate capture.

Avoid automatically converting it into:

```text
"This proves something
is wrong with me."
```

or:

```text
"This proves external reality
changed."
```

The protocol preserves both observer and external explanations as hypotheses where relevant.

---

# Replication

Where possible, ask whether the observation can be repeated.

```text
Same observer?

Different observer?

Same context?

Different context?

Same representation?

Different representation?
```

Replication conditions should be documented.

---

# Independence

Cross-observer agreement becomes more informative when observers are meaningfully independent.

Ask:

```text
Did they see each other's answers?

Did they share instructions?

Did they share the same representation?

Did they share prior expectations?
```

Agreement remains evidence.

Its interpretation depends on conditions.

---

# Controls

Where experimental testing is possible, comparison conditions may include:

```text
baseline

no-trigger condition

alternative representation

unrelated cue

surface-similar cue

different observer condition

different context
```

Controls should match the specific hypothesis.

There is no universal control condition for all Re-Ignition observations.

---

# Discriminator

A discriminator answers:

```text
What result would favor
H1 over H2?
```

For example:

```text
H1
representation change

H2
physical structure change
```

A useful discriminator might ask what:

```text
external measurement
```

should differ between the two.

The exact discriminator depends on the hypothesis set.

---

# Failure Condition

Every preferred model should attempt to answer:

```text
What would make this
less likely?
```

A model without a meaningful failure condition may not yet be operational enough for testing.

That is acceptable.

Record:

```text
failure condition:
not yet operationalized
```

rather than inventing one.

---

# Minimum Supported Claim

At the end of every observation cycle, write:

```text
MINIMUM SUPPORTED CLAIM
```

This should be the smallest statement that:

```text
preserves the observation

does not erase uncertainty

does not assume mechanism

and can survive current evidence
```

This field is one of the protocol's primary anti-drift tools.

---

# Example Claim Separation

Suppose:

```text
Experience:

"I suddenly remembered
another timeline."
```

Possible protocol decomposition:

```text
OBSERVATION

A temporal representation
became newly accessible.
```

```text
INTERPRETATION

The representation feels like
another history.
```

```text
HYPOTHESIS 1

Memory reconstruction.
```

```text
HYPOTHESIS 2

Representation change.
```

```text
HYPOTHESIS 3

Projection difference.
```

```text
HYPOTHESIS 4

Distinct physical timeline.
```

```text
CURRENT STATUS

Unresolved.
```

The protocol preserves the experience without forcing its ontology.

---

# Example Re-Ignition Capture

Suppose a student reports:

```text
"I saw an old kind of problem
and suddenly remembered
how to solve it."
```

Record:

```text
EARLIER ACCESS

Student previously demonstrated
the method.
```

```text
BASELINE

Student initially could not
produce the method.
```

```text
TRIGGER

Old problem format.
```

```text
RECOGNITION

Student identified the earlier
problem-solving relationship.
```

```text
MINIMUM CLAIM

Exposure to the old problem format
preceded renewed functional access.
```

Then test:

```text
Can the student solve
a new problem without
the original cue?
```

This helps distinguish immediate cue dependence from stabilization.

---

# Relationship to Comparative Observer Test

The Observation Protocol provides the record structure used by:

```text
./comparative-observer-test.md
```

That experiment focuses specifically on:

```text
differences across observers
```

while this protocol applies more broadly.

---

# Relationship to Resonance Recall Test

The Observation Protocol provides the claim-separation structure used by:

```text
./resonance-recall-test.md
```

The Resonance Recall Test adds:

```text
baseline

cue conditions

recognition

recall

reconstruction

transfer

delayed retest
```

---

# Relationship to Student Simulation

The Student Simulation adapts this protocol for educational reasoning exercises.

```text
FIRST PASS
    ↓
OBSERVER PASS
    ↓
TRIADIC PASS
    ↓
COMPARISON
```

The Observation Protocol supplies the discipline underlying those passes.

---

# Relationship to the Experiments Branch

The experiments layer can be organized as:

```text
OBSERVATION PROTOCOL
      ↓
How do we capture cleanly?

COMPARATIVE OBSERVER TEST
      ↓
What changes across observers?

RESONANCE RECALL TEST
      ↓
What changes after a cue?

STUDENT SIMULATION
      ↓
What changes across
reasoning regimes?
```

Together:

```text
CAPTURE
  ↓
COMPARE
  ↓
TRIGGER
  ↓
TEST
  ↓
TEACH
```

---

# Research Questions

1. How reliably can observation and interpretation be separated?

2. How quickly does retrospective narrative alter event reports?

3. Does immediate capture improve preservation of first-signal information?

4. Which observer variables materially affect Re-Ignition reports?

5. Can cross-form invariants distinguish structural relationships from representation effects?

6. Can temporal anchoring reduce timeline-revision drift?

7. Can independent observers reproduce the same invariant?

8. Does the Minimum Supported Claim reduce overinterpretation?

9. Does explicit `UNKNOWN` improve later revision?

10. Can divergence-point analysis identify the layer where models separate?

11. Does preserving failed hypotheses improve later reasoning?

12. Can paradox preservation reduce premature binary collapse?

13. What observation categories require domain-specific protocols?

14. How should subjective resonance reports be compared with task performance?

15. Can first-signal capture distinguish recognition from retrospective reconstruction?

16. When does observer-state recording add useful discrimination?

17. When does it add unnecessary complexity?

18. Which parts of the protocol improve experimental reproducibility?

19. Can the protocol be used effectively without Triadic terminology?

20. What results would demonstrate that parts of the protocol should be removed or simplified?

---

# Boundary Conditions

The Observation Protocol does **not by itself establish**:

```text
the truth of an observation

the accuracy of memory

causation

mechanism

hidden structure

a hidden observer

Formless ontology

timeline alteration

multiple physical timelines

Universe as Operator

or any specific metaphysical claim
```

It also does not guarantee that introspective capture perfectly preserves an internal event.

The minimum purpose is:

> **Preserve observations, access conditions, representations, interpretations, competing hypotheses, and uncertainty clearly enough that later comparison and testing remain possible.**

# Working Summary

The Observation Protocol begins with:

```text
SOMETHING HAPPENED
```

and refuses to let that become immediately:

```text
THEREFORE I KNOW WHY
```

Instead:

```text
OBSERVE
   ↓
CAPTURE
   ↓
ANCHOR
   ↓
LOCATE THE OBSERVER
   ↓
IDENTIFY THE FORM
   ↓
SEPARATE INTERPRETATION
   ↓
FIND INVARIANTS
   ↓
LOCATE DIVERGENCE
   ↓
PRESERVE PARADOX
   ↓
GENERATE ALTERNATIVES
   ↓
DEFINE DISCRIMINATORS
   ↓
TEST
   ↓
REVISIT
   ↓
REVISE
```

Its permanent guardrails are:

```text
CAPTURE
    ≠
PROOF
```

```text
TRIGGER
    ≠
CAUSE
```

```text
RESONANCE
    ≠
CAUSATION
```

```text
RECOGNITION
    ≠
VERIFICATION
```

```text
LOCAL
    ≠
GLOBAL
```

```text
FORM
    ≠
COMPLETE STRUCTURE
```

```text
FORMLESS
    ≠
HIDDEN REALITY PROVEN
```

```text
STABILIZATION
    ≠
TRUTH
```

The guiding discipline is:

> **Capture before story.  
> Anchor before inference.  
> Locate the observer before assigning the difference.  
> Preserve the first form before revision changes it.  
> Search for invariants before choosing a mechanism.  
> Keep alternatives alive until a discriminator separates them.  
> Record unknown when unknown is the most accurate answer.**

In its smallest form:

```text
WHAT HAPPENED?
      ↓
WHAT CHANGED?
      ↓
WHAT STAYED THE SAME?
      ↓
WHAT ELSE COULD EXPLAIN IT?
      ↓
WHAT CAN WE CHECK?
```

The protocol does not make the observation true.

**It keeps the observation clean enough that truth can still be investigated.**


Main writing choice: I made this the module’s experimental root protocol, rather than another experiment competing beside the others. comparative-observer-test.md, resonance-recall-test.md, and student-simulation.md can now all be understood as specialized extensions of this same sequence: capture → anchor → separate → compare → test → revisit.
